item.title: In assessing GOP midterm losses, Trump says his supporters likely didn't vote
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Days after Republicans faced a series of bruising midterm election losses, President Trump stood by his handling of the economy and the Iran war — but he acknowledged some "bad messaging" on economic issues and said his immigration crackdown was "too tough" at times. In a sitdown with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat, the president also suggested some top administration officials could be on their way out. One hour later, he announced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles would depart her role and be replaced by Stephen Miller. Here are the biggest takeaways from the interview: Why did Republicans lose? Republicans lost more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats on Tuesday, with some races still uncalled, including in places that Mr. Trump won by double-digit margins two years ago. About 63% of midterm voters disapproved of Mr. Trump's job performance, and 44% said one reason for their vote was to express opposition to him, according to CBS News exit polling. Asked for his analysis of the midterm losses, Mr. Trump told 60 Minutes that voters "didn't like the war" with Iran or the soaring gas prices that it triggered. But he said he believes the primary reason for Republicans' losses was that "I was not on the ballot," an explanation he has offered several times in recent days. He suggested his pre-election endorsements and rallies "brought a lot of people … a lot closer to victory." Ahead of Election Day, the president frequently urged his supporters to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." So, what happened? "I think they didn't vote, really. I think they didn't vote. I think in some cases, they didn't like the candidates. And that's, you know, their prerogative," he said. Some of the candidates were picked by the president. He endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Lone Star State's bitter GOP Senate primary, and he endorsed Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother's South Carolina Senate seat — encouraging her to run for a full term. Mr. Trump argued that "Cornyn would have lost also." Economic performance has been "phenomenal," but "we couldn't get the word across" The president defended his stewardship of the economy in his 60 Minutes sitdown, which came hours after a stronger-than-expected jobs report . He said "the numbers are phenomenal." "We're doing numbers that have never been done before. 401(k)s are at their all-time high by a lot. Under other presidents, they were a disaster. 401(k)s have made people rich," the president said. Pressed on the fact that not all Americans have large retirement accounts, Mr. Trump responded: "But a lot of people do." But exit polling shows three-fourths of midterm voters viewed the condition of the economy as either poor or not so good — and 70% of that group voted for Democratic House candidates. Voters were especially concerned about prices of gasoline, food, utilities and healthcare, and two-thirds of voters believed that Mr. Trump's tariff policies hurt the country's economy. Mr. Trump said the problem is that "we couldn't get the word across." "I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me, but I would talk about it all the time. So I don't know, how much can I talk about it?" the president said. He predicted that Americans are "going to notice it in the next two, three, four months," arguing that his policies will lead to a resurgence of manufacturing jobs. "I'm not looking to" escalate Iran war The morning after the election, Vice President JD Vance argued on social media "the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone" — the broadly unpopular Iran war." Mr. Trump said Vance told him about his plan to write that post, and he responded: "You write what you want." The president said "I don't disagree" with the vice president's diagnosis for why the Republicans lost the midterms, "other than one thing." "The one thing he left out is — that I would say, and maybe he wouldn't say it, I don't know. I've never asked him really. But, if you had … to do again, would you do it? And that's Iran. Would you go and attack Iran?" he said. The president said his answer to that question is an "emphatic yes," arguing Iran's conventional military has been degraded and its nuclear program has been set back. "I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not? But … I have to go with what's right for our country," he said. "If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what's happened." In a visit to the Oval Office later in the day, Mr. Trump reiterated his view that historians will judge the Iran war more favorably than voters. He pointed out a portrait of Ulysses S. Grant, a former president whose reputation has improved with age . "I mean, he was very low on the list and now he's much higher on the list," Mr. Trump said. "I think as an example — the fact that I have taken the nuclear weapon away from Iran will not be good, short-term. But long-term, I think it's going to be very important." Since September, Iran and the U.S. have largely held off from major attacks, though the U.S. launched a set of limited defensive strikes on Iranian targets earlier this week. Mr. Trump has suggested in recent months that the war could ramp up again after the election, but he has also frequently predicted Iran is interested in striking a deal, and Qatar is mediating a diplomatic push between the two sides. He told 60 Minutes he believes Iran is close to striking a deal, but the outcome of the election "gives them a little bit of a hope certificate." Asked if he plans to escalate the war now that the midterms are over, the president said: "Well, I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to." On deportation policy, Trump says "I think it was too tough" Mr. Trump's victory in 2024 was fueled in part by voters' discontent with the Biden administration's immigration policies. But this year, exit polling shows 58% think the Trump administration's actions on immigration have gone too far. In battlegrounds like Texas, many Latino voters who shifted to Mr. Trump two years ago pivoted back to Democrats due to concerns about immigration policy . The president said immigration "both helped and hurt." "I think I got an A+ for closing up the border," he said. So, which immigration policies hurt him? "For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump said. "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally." He continued: "Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes." "I think it was too tough," the president said of his deportation policies. Mr. Trump's plans for the second half of his term aren't clear. On Friday, he replaced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, a hardliner who is widely viewed as an architect of the Trump administration's immigration enforcement strategy. Last year, he pressed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to conduct at least 3,000 arrests per day . The president said he'd "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats. "I devote almost no time to my net worth" Mr. Trump is the wealthiest person to hold the presidency, and his wealth has grown by billions in recent years, fueled partly by his family's cryptocurrency ventures . Polls show many voters believe the president is prioritizing his personal business interests while in office. Asked about reporting by Forbes that his net worth has soared since he returned to the White House, Mr. Trump said, "So did everyone." (Douthat noted that, unlike Mr. Trump, his net worth hasn't gone up by nearly $3 billion. The president responded, "Well, you should've had stock.") "I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care," he said. "I have a lot of money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know." He denied that he is prioritizing his own financial interests, saying his stock holdings are invested in broad indexes and his sons are in charge of his company. "I have a company. My sons run the company. It's hard to say to them, 'Don't do anything anymore for four years because I'm president," he said. He also said "every president has had this problem" where people leave the administration to work in private industry, and "no matter what they do, there's a conflict." Will any administration officials be fired? Trump says he'll "be doing maybe a few changes" Mr. Trump spoke with 60 Minutes shortly before announcing Wiles' departure. During the interview, he hinted at impending personnel changes . Asked whether he expected to fire anyone after Republicans' midterm losses, he said: "I do, yeah. Little bit." He added that "I love my Cabinet," but "I'll … be doing maybe a few changes." Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday night, CBS News reported . CBS News also reported this week that Mr. Trump has asked aides whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay in his role. The president told 60 Minutes he has confidence in Hegseth, and pushed back against calls from Democrats to impeach the Pentagon chief. "They want to impeach him. Very unfair," Mr. Trump said. "We had two wars, we won both. We won Venezuela, we won Iran." Trump will "probably" endorse a successor, but "not necessarily" With the 2028 presidential election now two years away, both Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are widely seen as possible heirs to Mr. Trump's political movement. The president has often joked about the succession guessing games. Asked if he plans to endorse a 2028 Republican primary candidate, Mr. Trump said "probably," but "not necessarily." He said the Republicans "have a tremendous bench" and "I have so many people that I have great relationships with." Aside from Rubio and Vance, he said "there's some senators that are excellent." "I may or may not get involved. I don't know," he said. "Maybe I'm better off not getting involved. I think it would play a big role if I did, because my endorsement capacity has been very strong." Trump planning "tremendous numbers of pardons" Mr. Trump said he plans to keep using his pardon power aggressively before leaving office. "I don't want to have good people that are serving this country and doing a great job spending the rest of their life, like I had to do for four years, defending myself by radical left lunatics, by people that were very nasty and mean. I intend to issue tremendous numbers of pardons," he said, joking that "anybody that got within a thousand miles of the Oval Office" could get one. The president said he doesn't expect to attempt the legally untested maneuver of pardoning himself, but "it's certainly not unreasonable." He also said: "I pardoned the J6ers. I don't think any group's been treated more unfairly than them, and to this day, when they see me they cry." Asked about the Jan. 6 rioters who attacked police officers, he argued that "there were some that got rough, but, you know, they were rough to them, too." Trump on UFOs: Military pilots have "told me things that are very strange" The president said one of the most frequent questions he gets is about what the military calls unexplained anomalous phenomena — better known as unidentified flying objects, or UFOs. Earlier this year, Mr. Trump signed an executive order mandating the release of sensitive files on UAP sightings , leading the Pentagon to disclose photos, videos and investigative reports on what appear to be unexplained, often strange objects in the sky. "I'm not too much of a believer, but I sat in the Oval Office, first term and a little bit second term, meeting with Air Force pilots that are really good, solid people. These are not people that you would say are conspiracy theorists. They don't even know what it means. But they're great, great pilots. Young, handsome. They have beautiful, nice flat tops. I'd like to have a haircut just like them. They look perfect, like Tom Cruise. … They're thin, you know, very thin and very everything. And … they're the real deal. And they've told me things that are very strange." Could Trump forgive his enemies? Toward the end of the sitdown, Douthat asked Mr. Trump — who has survived multiple assassination attempts — what he thinks will happen when he dies. "Well, I hope I'm missed," he responded. That wasn't exactly what Douthat meant. "Well, I'm a religious person, so in theory, I go to heaven," the president said. "I hope so. I don't want to go to hell." Douthat asked whether Mr. Trump could forgive his political foes in order to get into heaven. "The answer is no. I want to be honest, no." Pressed further, he said the "easy answer" would be to say yes, but he acknowledged: "I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and always will." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/10-takeaways-from-trump-60-minutes-interview/

item.title: Former RFK Jr. adviser accuses several White House officials of corruption
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The full transcript of Margaret Brennan's interview with Calley Means is available on cbsnews.com. A former senior White House adviser and top aide to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is accusing several Trump administration officials, including the recently resigned White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, of prioritizing industry interests over the health of voters as part of the White House's midterm elections strategy. "Underneath Trump's nose, in many cases, you had a group of former lobbyists, catering to the vaping industry, catering to the ultra-processed food industry, catering to the pharmaceutical industry, catering to the pesticide industry and doing their bidding with an excuse that we need their money for the midterms and really need to actually go against what voters said," Calley Means told "Face the Nation" moderator Margaret Brennan in an interview that aired Sunday. Means helped found the "Make America Healthy Again" movement and helped form the winning alliance between Mr. Trump and Kennedy in 2024 before serving as Kennedy's top aide. Means helped lead the Department of Health and Human Services' efforts to revise the country's dietary guidelines and remove soda and candy from SNAP benefits before resigning last month. He told CBS News that Wiles and "a very close-knit crew" of other White House advisers "were taking money from the industries we ran on fighting against." Means went public Friday with very specific allegations of corruption against Wiles and a call for President Trump to "clear his house" in an interview he taped Thursday for "The Joe Rogan Experience" podcast. He claimed Wiles and her deputy, James Blair, relentlessly pushed HHS to find a pathway to approve fruit-flavored vapes. In early May, the Food and Drug Administration approved some fruit-flavored e-cigarettes. Blair denied Means' characterization of his role in the vape debate in a statement to CBS News. "I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair said. "I was tasked with driving FDA to make its process for approving or denying nicotine delivery device applications work the way current federal law dictates it works, which is that applicants get a yes or no answer on approval in six months. Calley is intentionally misrepresenting my role and my responsibility because he opposes the issue entirely. Even though the president himself has made his position on smoking and smoking alternatives known very publicly and has provided clear direction. Calley just doesn't like it." Two sources familiar with the process told CBS News that Blair was tasked by Mr. Trump with driving then-FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary to more quickly respond to applications from the nicotine industry, but also acknowledged that the president sought to make flavored vapes more available. As a 2024 presidential candidate, Mr. Trump vowed to "save" vaping and mentioned his past efforts on behalf of flavored vaping during his first administration, which he said in a social media post was intended to get people off smoking. Mr. Trump won backing from e-cigarette companies, shop owners and vaping enthusiasts. In May, Makary was pressed to resign his post as FDA commissioner amid reports that he had been pressured by the White House to approve the fruit-flavored vapes. "Big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials to put repeated pressure on me to approve fruit-flavored vapes that appeal to children—I wouldn't do it," Makary said in a statement to CBS News. "The Kratom/7-OH lobby ran the same playbook to undermine my efforts to make this new 'gas station heroin' illegal. As FDA commissioner, I always rejected political corruption just as voters across the political spectrum did last week." Multiple sources confirmed to CBS News the New York Times' reporting in May that tobacco lobbyists had been at the president's Florida golf course with him at lunch and pushed him on the way e-cigarettes were being regulated by the FDA. Means claimed Wiles set up the meeting. Wiles submitted her resignation to Mr. Trump on Thursday night, a U.S. official and a senior White House adviser told CBS News. Her resignation was tied to Republicans' midterm defeats , according to three sources familiar with the matter. The departure became public shortly after Mr. Trump taped an interview with 60 Minutes midday Friday. When asked if it was his intention to get Wiles removed from her position, Means responded, "Yes. I think President Trump has been subverted by people that are beholden to special interests and not what President Trump ran on, and what voters voted for." It is not clear at this time whether the public remarks factored into the president's decision to expedite Wiles' departure. In a statement to CBS News, Wiles denied Means' allegations that she arranged for tobacco industry representatives to meet with the president at his golf course to discuss vape policy. Earlier this year, Mr. Trump signed an executive order to boost production of glyphosate, a herbicide that is included in the weedkiller Roundup and which has been found to be linked to cancer. WHO has deemed glyphosate to be "probably carcinogenic to humans." For decades as a private attorney, Kennedy had spearheaded a legal challenge to the chemical giant Monsanto for its use of the herbicide. In a statement on social media at the time of the president's order, Kennedy said: "Our agricultural system depends heavily on these chemicals." Kennedy testified to Congress in March that he was "very clear with the president about my own displeasure with the executive order." Kennedy said in that testimony the executive order on glyphosate "came from the Pentagon," and "the president felt it was necessary for national security reasons." In June, the Supreme Court sided with Monsanto, ruling that it cannot be held liable for failing to warn consumers about alleged cancer risks in Roundup. On "Face the Nation," Means accused White House adviser Heidi Overton of working with the Department of Justice to write a brief to the Supreme Court, urging them to take the case prior to Mr. Trump's executive order. A senior White House official told CBS News that the solicitor general wrote the brief for the Supreme Court at the request of the court. The official also said that Dr. Overton did weigh in on the brief in the final stages but just made changes to "tone." The Trump administration argued in court filings that federal standards supersede state-level liability claims, which was the same position taken by glyphosate-maker Monsanto, now known as Bayer. There is an ongoing EPA review of glyphosate, expected to conclude in early 2027. Means alleged the prior EPA review of glyphosate was "thrown out because it had ghostwritten research showing Bayer bribed EPA officials." Means resigned last month and said he is leaving "with tremendous respect for President Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr." Food stocks rallied on the day of his departure. Means told "Face the Nation" that he was frustrated with his stalled efforts to create a federal definition of ultra-processed food, which he argues is poisoning American children. "There was relentless lobbying against this because the industry and they said this in meetings with me and other people, they just don't want a definition because they don't want Americans to have more transparency into what they're eating because there's a shift away from ultra-processed food right now." Means said on "Face the Nation" that he is confident of Mr. Trump's stance on the "issue of improving health for children," but claimed that the president's advisers gave him poor advice and "treated him like a baby in many respects and used him." "They would block access to and information to him all the time," Means alleged. "I would be not surprised at all, you know, if they had very short conversations on these issues, you know, where the president's extremely busy and the president said, 'OK, whatever.'" Mr. Trump's top adviser Stephen Miller , who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, wasn't among them, according to Means. "Stephen Miller wants to get transformative things done with Bobby Kennedy and President Trump that are not partisan, but structural," he said. "He wants to get the same things done that Elizabeth Warren and (Abdul) El-Sayed and other people are running on. And I think there is a major opportunity to come together and get some big things done, which, quite frankly, we have to do." In August, Mr. Trump nominated policy aide Dr. Heidi Overton to be the next FDA commissioner. Kennedy has endorsed Overton's nomination. However, Means told CBS News that Overton "was the biggest block to MAHA policies I encountered in the government," alleging she "did whatever" Wiles "told her to do." Means alleged that in one particular meeting, Overton told Makary — whom Means described as Overton's "mentor" — that she "couldn't help" him on other policies unless he approved "a drug that he thought scientifically should not be approved," Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine, mFLUSIVA. In August, the FDA approved mFLUSIVA for adults ages 50 and older. It was the first influenza vaccine using mRNA technology to receive FDA approval. The approval came despite repeated criticism of mRNA technology by Kennedy, who in 2025 canceled 22 vaccine development projects that use mRNA technology. The FDA had earlier this year said it would refuse to consider Moderna's application. But it reversed course about a week later. Clinical trials found mFLUSIVA to be slightly more effective than the standard flu shot. "It's just a factual statement that after Marty left, partly due to the vaping issue, she drove the creation of the relaxed vaping strategy," Means said, adding that he does not believe Overton has the "character or integrity" to be FDA commissioner. A spokesman for Overton responded to Means' criticism of her qualifications and told CBS News that "two former FDA commissioners think otherwise." Calley Means is the brother of Dr. Casey Means, also a close ally of Kennedy. CBS News previously reported that both played a key role in coordinating Kennedy's endorsement of Mr. Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign. Casey Means was briefly Mr. Trump's pick for surgeon general, but her name was withdrawn in April because her bid stalled in the Senate. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/calley-means-white-house-health-and-human-services-rfk-jr/

item.title: Adam Hamilton says he'd be 'deeply disappointed' if Dems focus on investigating Trump
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, who flipped deep-red Kansas for Democrats, said Sunday that he hopes to prioritize lowering costs for his constituents in the next Congress and that he would be “deeply disappointed” to spend two years investigating members of the Trump administration. “The bigger priority for me, and I think for most people in America, especially people living paycheck to paycheck, is ‘please help us with the cost of living,’” Hamilton told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” Specifically, he said the new Congress should immediately focus on ending the war in Iran and “claw[ing] back tariffs policies.” “If I spent the next two years — my first two years in the Senate — in investigations, I’d be deeply disappointed. I want to get to work helping the people in my state and helping the people across the country,” Hamilton said. After their landslide victories Tuesday gave Democrats control of the House and the Senate in the next Congress, newly elected leaders and those who were re-elected are turning to focus on their priorities for the next two years. Many are calling on colleagues to focus on an affordability agenda, but some senior leaders have said they’ll also prioritize oversight and investigations into possible corruption by President Donald Trump and his allies. “Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters Wednesday. Several Democrats, including Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who was an impeachment manager for one of Trump’s impeachments during his first term, have floated potentially impeaching him for a third time. Hamilton said Sunday, “I’m not as interested in impeachment as setting up guardrails.” But he added, “I understand the move and the desire to do this.” Instead, he said his party should concentrate on making life more affordable for Americans. “Let’s focus on helping the American people,” he said. “And I’ll tell you, the Democrats, if they don’t, if we don’t figure that out and get to work on helping people, this is going to be a one-and-done, kind of, you know, kind of blue wave.” Appearing later on the program, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., agreed with Hamilton. “I think the senator-elect, Hamilton, made a good point,” Sanders told “Meet the Press,” adding: “We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump. We have to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.” With Democrats winning in 54 Senate seats and two more Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled, Schumer could be poised to take over as majority leader in the next Congress if a majority of the Democratic members of the Senate vote in his favor. Hamilton has said he doesn’t plan to support Schumer’s bid to be majority leader. On Sunday, he said he has “no disrespect for Chuck Schumer,” but “I just really don’t [want him as majority leader], and I’ve told him that, as well.” Hamilton cited the volume of TV ads during the campaign linking him to Schumer, which he said addressed the fact that “a lot of people in Kansas feel, who may not know Chuck Schumer personally, who don’t know him personally, but you know that they perceive him to be further to the left and somebody who’s a divisive figure.” He demurred when he was asked whom he might support over Schumer, saying: “I know probably 10 senators personally, and even those I only know from brief conversations. So, you know, I’m not at a place where I can tell you these are, this is my short list.” He added: “There are a handful of people that I think are probably, you know, lead more from the center, but I don’t know enough yet to be able to say these are the people I would endorse.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/sen-adam-hamilton-disappointed-democrats-trump-investigations-schumer-rcna608088

item.title: Dems set sights on Stephen Miller, Elon Musk and corporate America after midterms rout
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Tim Reid WASHINGTON, Nov 8 (Reuters) - Tech megabillionaire Elon Musk and President Donald Trump's newly appointed White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, and some large companies will likely be targets of congressional probes when Democrats take control of Congress in ‌January, senior lawmakers said on Sunday. In television appearances, US Representative Robert Garcia of California and US Senator Elizabeth Warren of ‌Massachusetts, set to lead the House Oversight and Senate Banking committees, vowed aggressive oversight after their party's sweeping midterm election victory. Meanwhile, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries indicated he and his ​fellow Democrats would back an impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Garcia, who is the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said investigations will focus on Musk's involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency's firing of federal workers last year, and Miller's role in Trump's hardline immigration crackdown. "I think there's a lot of interest, not just from our committee, but from committees across the Congress to speak to Mr. Musk," Garcia told CNN's "State of the Union." Warren said some ‌companies should be ready for congressional investigations. She did ⁠not name any of the companies. "If you've been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you'd better get ready for some investigations, serious ones," Warren told CBS's "Face the Nation" program. DEMOCRATS FOCUS ON MILLER, ⁠HEGSETH Miller — whom Garcia called the architect of a "horrific, unjust" immigration policy — has been promoted to White House chief of staff. "Stephen Miller is at the center of the major policy decisions that are happening in the administration, and so it does deserve oversight and investigation," Garcia told CNN. Voters delivered a historic rebuke to ​Republicans in ​Tuesday's midterm election, but with Miller as White House chief of staff, the ​Trump administration is expected to continue its aggressive approach ‌to immigration enforcement, amplify cultural conflicts and give no ground to a Democratic-controlled Congress, say officials and experts who spoke to Reuters. The crackdown on immigration, which included operations in which two people were fatally shot in Minnesota by federal agents, has proven widely unpopular. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in October found that only 37% approved of Trump's handling of immigration, down from 50% when he took office. Jeffries, who will become speaker of the US House in January, said on Sunday that Democrats would support a measure to impeach Hegseth, a congressional process that could remove him from ‌office. Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican and Trump critic who leaves Congress in ​January after a Trump-backed primary defeat this year, has said he will reintroduce articles ​of impeachment against Hegseth soon. Jeffries said he is a "hard ​yes" on backing that measure. "Pete Hegseth has got to go," Jeffries told ABC's "This Week," citing the defense secretary's oversight of ‌the unpopular Iran war launched by Trump in February, which ​has led to a spike in ​gas prices. "I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution," Jeffries added. Attorney General Todd Blanche signaled on Sunday that the Trump administration was prepared to battle the Democrats in Congress, calling threats by some Democrats to target administration officials and allies "not ​something we can tolerate in this country." "If that's ‌what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready," said Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump. "If you ​work in this administration, you have a lawyer. It's me." (Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington; Additional reporting by Abigail Summerville, ​Brad Heath and Tom Polansek; Editing by Sergio Non and Nia Williams) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/democrats-eye-musk-miller-probes-162946969.html

item.title: MAGA voters at a Trump rally eye contenders to lead the GOP in 2028
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
With Democrats taking control of Congress in the midterm elections, MAGA voters are already sizing up potential successors to President Donald Trump in 2028 — with Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeatedly emerging as favorites among those interviewed by Fox News Digital. "I like [Rubio]," one American told Fox News Digital. "I like that he's no-nonsense, similar to Trump." "Well, I like JD Vance obviously," another said. "I like Marco Rubio. There's some other ones, too, that are maybe not so much mainstream that are coming up that I like too." Trump Told Donors 'We Need To Elect Jd,' Source Confirms, As He Weighs Vance Or Rubio In 2028 Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are gaining traction among American voters as potential favorable 2028 presidential candidates for Republicans. "JD is great too, but Rubio has a little more experience," one said. "He's articulate, he’s well-spoken. He's got good ideas. I just really like him." Fox News Digital spoke with Americans attending a Trump rally in Port Huron, Michigan, as one of Trump’s final stops before Tuesday’s midterms that ended in a stunning blue wave. Fueled by anger over high costs and the war with Iran , Americans voted to oust Trump and his agenda, boosting Democrats to large majorities in the House and Senate. Read On The Fox News App With Democrats looking to rebuke Trump and his allies, Republicans that Fox News Digital spoke with are looking for a presidential candidate to fill in Trump’s "footsteps." "I'm really open to see who can fill Trump's footsteps, not just the next person in line," one told Fox News Digital. Fox News/norc Study: Voters Look To 2028 Focused On The Economy Sen. Chuck Schumer said President Donald Trump, seen on Oct. 28, 2026, would be the subject of Senate investigations whenever he violates the law. "I wish Trump could run again," another said. Another brought up the prospect of another presidential run by Gov. Ron DeSantis , R-Fla., who has tried to distance himself from the results of Tuesday’s midterms. item.title: Netanyahu rival Eisenkot seeks 'wide' government, but his path to power is uncertain
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Steven Scheer JERUSALEM, Nov 8 (Reuters) - Former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot said on Sunday he will work to form a wide government as quickly as possible, but his path to power was uncertain following a deadlocked election that failed to dislodge Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Israeli ‌President Isaac Herzog on Saturday gave Eisenkot the first opportunity to try to form a new government after the October 27 election left both Eisenkot ‌and Netanyahu short of the majority needed to govern. Herzog officially handed Eisenkot the task on Sunday at a meeting at the president's residence, starting the clock on what Eisenkot said would be an "extraordinarily complex" ​process. "We are in a state of emergency, approaching a point of no return for the State of Israel," Eisenkot said. "We must form a national emergency government. This will require creative and unconventional political steps." Eisenkot said Israeli democracy was at a vulnerable moment at a time when it faced immense challenges, with Herzog citing a threat of attack from Iran, the need to progress towards peace in Gaza and negotiations with Lebanon and other neighbours. "There is great urgency for new leadership, leadership that people can look in the eye ‌and trust," Eisenkot said. His potential pathways to power include trying ⁠to form a minority government with Arab party support for key issues; forming a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties that he and his allies have shunned in the past; or forging a unity government with Netanyahu. All three options face formidable obstacles. NEGOTIATIONS COULD TAKE ⁠SIX WEEKS Eisenkot said he will call on all parties to join who meet his main principles. These include recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; a duty of national service for all to strengthen the military and expand its ranks; and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization and a commitment to destroying its military and governing capacity. "I am ​convinced ​that it is possible and right to form a new government quickly, one that will win ​a large majority in the Knesset," Eisenkot said, referring to Israel's ‌parliament. Eisenkot now has 28 days plus a possible 14-day extension. If he fails, Netanyahu will likely get his shot at forming a government. Should he also be unable, new elections could be called. Herzog, who consulted with all parties, said Eisenkot received the "clear and unequivocal support" of a majority of lawmakers on who has the better chance of forming the next government that will win the confidence of the Knesset. Netanyahu's Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu's wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total, short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. Eisenkot's Yashar party emerged as the second-largest party with 21 ‌seats, while his coalition, spanning four centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led parties, won just 48 seats. Two ​parties representing Israel's Arab minority won an unprecedented 19 seats. LIEBERMAN SAYS HE COULD WORK WITH ​ULTRA-ORTHODOX PARTIES Netanyahu called for a unity government of all Zionist parties to preserve ​a Jewish state, while giving no indication whether he would was prepared to serve under Eisekenkot's leadership. "This is the will of the ‌people and the need of the hour," he said in ​a statement, ruling out a coalition government with Arabs - ​who make up 21% of Israel's population. Potentially making Eisenkot's job tougher is the position of one opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman of the Israel Our Home party, who has ruled out a unity government with Netanyahu or a minority government that has backing from Arab parties. But Lieberman has softened his stance ​on sitting with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties as long as they ‌agree to support a law under which ultra-Orthodox men serve in the military. "Given the current reality, in order to prevent further elections and bring ​an end to the Netanyahu era, there is no choice but to make difficult decisions and resolve issues where flexibility is possible and ​common ground can be found," Lieberman said. (Reporting by Steven Scheer; editing by Philippa Fletcher) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/netanyahu-rival-eisenkot-seeks-wide-173553169.html

item.title: Russell Brand facing lengthy prison term as he awaits sentencing for rape
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand faces a reckoning Monday for sexual abuse that occurred just offstage from a public life built around boasts of his erotic exploits. Brand, 51, faces a significant prison term after being convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. The British actor-comedian known for outrageous stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol asserted that he was innocent and all his encounters were consensual. But a jury of eight men and four women did not buy his defense and found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers on allegations dating back to 2004. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. Brand was partly damned by his own words about his obsession with sex and his well-documented life of promiscuity. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones called Brand a ruthless, calculating, manipulative “sexual predator” who treated women as a “disposable commodity.” She quoted from his 2007 memoir “My Booky Wook” to illustrate how his insatiable sex drive led him to cross the line. “If I want something — whether it’s a job or a woman — I will determinedly, resolutely, remove anything that’s in the way, until I possess the object of my desire,” he wrote. The accusers came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4 that aired accusations from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand . Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, but cleared of orally raping her in a restroom. He was also found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 and of anally raping a fan at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009. The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009. Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party’s annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men’s bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV. The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life. Brand, who was known for edgy stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, rose to prominence in the early 2000s hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry. In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion. item.title: 8-year-old Haitian boy in federal custody after ICE check-in
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
An 8-year-old Haitian boy who lost Temporary Protected Status earlier this year was taken into federal custody after an immigration check-in, according to local advocates and school officials. The third grader, who attends Fay Elementary School in San Diego, was placed into government custody alone after attending an Immigration and Customs Enforcement appointment with his uncle on Thursday, according to his school district and an advocacy group. “The eight-year-old received a letter to meet with an ICE agent,” the San Diego Unified School District said in a letter to DHS. “His uncle, with whom he’s been living since the child’s father was deported more than a year ago, took him to meet the agent because he did not want to break the law.” New ICE facility to hold families, unaccompanied minors could open in Louisiana next week Advocates and school officials said the boy had been living with his uncle and cousins after his father was deported to Mexico last year. "They did not give the father the opportunity or chance to actually put in place legal guardianship for the kid," said Guerline Jozef, the executive director of the nonprofit Haitian Bridge Alliance. Cody Petterson, a board trustee with the SDUSD, told ABC News the uncle was designated on school records as an authorized caregiver. Charles Reed/ICE - PHOTO: An officer with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Dallas, Texas. A spokesperson for ICE told ABC News in a statement that because the uncle could not establish legal guardianship, agents treated the 8-year-old as an unaccompanied child under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, a federal law that provides protections for unaccompanied immigrant children. The agency did not allege any wrongdoing or abuse by the uncle, but invoked the law to mandate the child's transfer after designating him as an unaccompanied minor. "Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," the spokesperson said. According to the school district and an advocacy group, the 8-year-old remains in ORR custody. It is unclear if he will be removed from the U.S. Jozef called the detention "an excuse for [ICE] to remove the child and potentially put him in deportation proceedings.” Democrats press HHS over legal representation of migrant children “He was dressed very well, and he is very well cared for,” Jozef added. “There's absolutely no reason for them to remove him from the care of his relatives without putting in place proper procedures for him, knowing very well that ICE already deported the father.” In the letter to DHS, San Diego Unified School District officials said they have “witnessed situations in which children who should be attending school and participating in a supportive educational environment instead find themselves in government facilities.” “Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” the district said. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/US/8-year-haitian-boy-federal-custody-after-ice/story?id=137960678

item.title: Popular podcast sees sponsors flee after hosts laughed at Charlie Kirk joke
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A popular progressive podcast has seen its sponsors flee after laughing at a joke about the slain conservative influencer Charlie Kirk , which the hosts later admitted was “insensitive.” Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan read social media posts reacting to Tuesday’s midterm election — in which Democrats took control of the House and Senate and won key governors’ races — on Thursday’s episode of their I’ve Had It podcast. They both cracked up to a post that read, “We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again.” The clip has since been cut from the episode, and the two apologized for laughing at the joke. But the damage has already been done. Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk , blasted “leftist podcasters” and others who laugh about political assassination “beyond disgusting” in an X post Sunday. A popular progressive podcast has seen its sponsors flee after laughing at a joke about the slain conservative influencer Charlie Kirk, which the hosts later admitted was 'insensitive' (Getty) When an outraged social media user told his followers to boycott Cash App for sponsoring “these rotten women,” the peer-to-peer payment platform wrote on X Friday, “We do not condone violence of any kind, and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast.” Pet brand Chewy announced Saturday that it currently has no ties to the podcast. “We do not sponsor or support the ‘I’ve Had It’ podcast. We unequivocally condemn violence in all forms. The comments made by the hosts do not reflect Chewy’s values or what we stand for as a company,” Chewy wrote on X. Eyewear brand Zenni also announced that it “does not condone violence of any type.” “We have canceled advertising on I’ve Had It and are reviewing our podcast placements against our brand safety standards,” Zenni wrote on X. Organic bedding brand Boll & Branch said it “does not currently advertise with the ‘I’ve Had It’ podcast and will not in the future.” Payment platform Cash App, pet brand Chewy and other companies have announced they currently don’t have ties with podcast hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan, adding that they don’t condone violence (Getty) Kirk, the founder of the conservative youth organization Turning Point USA, was assassinated at age 31 during an outdoor event on a college campus in Utah in September 2025. Both Republicans and Democrats condemned the assassination of Kirk, who was seen as a steward of Trump’s MAGA movement and even a potential presidential nominee in the future. Some critics made light of or even celebrated Kirk’s death, and they were swiftly rebuked. Amid backlash for their response to a joke about Kirk’s assassination, Welch and Sullivan wrote on Instagram, “On Thursday’s show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk. It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize.” “Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence. We’ve long supported common-sense gun safety reform,” the hosts said. “To that end, we’ve made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety, the largest gun violence prevention organization in America. We’ll keep using our platforms to fight for the safety of all Americans.” This article originally appeared on The Independent at https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/ive-had-it-podcast-lose-sponsors-charlie-kirk-b3081273.html

item.title: Unreported votes give Republican the lead in Georgia state House race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ATLANTA, GEORGIA - JUNE 16: Voting stickers are laid out in the Buckhead Library polling station for the primary runoff election on June 16, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Jessica McGowan/Getty Images) Photo by: Jessica McGowan / Getty Images A vote-counting discrepancy in Seminole County has put a Republican incumbent ahead in a state legislative contest, prompting an investigation into how 388 votes went unreported on election night. A closely contested Georgia state House race has taken an unexpected turn after election officials identified 388 previously unreported votes in southwest Georgia, reversing the apparent outcome of a contest that could determine just how much power Democrats hold in the state legislature. The discrepancy involves Georgia House District 154, not the governor’s race or a congressional election. Republican incumbent Gerald Greene had been trailing Democratic challenger Harry James by just 58 votes following Tuesday’s election. But after the additional votes were included in Seminole Country’s totals, Greene moved ahead by 262 votes, according to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution . Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger has launched an investigation into why the votes were not included in the initial results and whether election officials followed required procedures. “This oversight didn’t just affect the numbers — it changed who was leading an election,” Raffensperger said. “That is unacceptable, and we intend to find out exactly how it happened.” The discrepancy was uncovered during routine post-election checks when state officials noticed that approximately 388 more voters had checked in at Seminole County polling places than the number of ballots reported as cast. Although initial reports described the issue as a missing memory card, Seminole County Elections Supervisor Ron Foskey disputed that characterization Saturday, saying all memory cards had been accounted for on election night. According to Foskey, the county’s election management system had not completed the final step necessary to validate and publish results from the last precinct’s memory card. Once that step was completed, the updated totals matched the county’s ballot scanner records. The county maintained that its chain-of-custody procedures were followed. State officials are investigating how the reporting error occurred. The implications extend beyond one legislative district. Democrats emerged from Tuesday’s election poised to control the Georgia House of Representatives for the first time in more than two decades. But the reversal in District 154 could leave the party with just 92 seats in the 180-member chamber, only one more than the 91 needed for a majority. Another legislative contest remains unresolved. Republican state Rep. Mike Cheokas faces Democrat Ethan Wolfe in a Dec. 1 runoff, leaving the chamber’s final balance of power unsettled. The District 154 contest is also significant because Greene, who was first elected as a Democrat in 1982 before switching parties after the 2010 election, is currently the only Republican in Georgia’s General Assembly representing a majority-Black district, according to the AJC. The corrected vote totals have not ended scrutiny of the election. Raffensperger’s office is examining what went wrong and what measures may be necessary to prevent similar reporting discrepancies in future elections. County officials face a Monday deadline to certify their election results. item.title: Trump says he was 'only kidding' about naming Dana White his new press secretary
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. President Donald Trump clarified Sunday afternoon that he was "only kidding" about his offer for UFC CEO Dana White to fulfill the open role of White House press secretary. Speaking to reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida, Trump expressed surprise at the reaction to his announcement and insisted his proposal was never meant to be taken seriously. However, the president also claimed that White was enthusiastic about the idea and confirmed the two are expected to meet Monday in Washington, D.C. Trump said the meeting was previously scheduled and concerned unrelated matters. Trump's full comments Sunday: "You would've thought that people would've said, 'He's having a good time.' I will tell you, I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea. And there's only one Dana, he's great. I don't know, you wouldn't mess around with him so much. So I was kidding, of course. When you look at the fighters that I put in [my post], that's why I said some don't come from our country, they come from parts unknown. They come from a lot of areas that are very rough areas. "So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy. So he's actually coming tomorrow. Of course I was kidding, and you could see that because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they're all going to come with him. I was just a little fun, but Dana is actually coming tomorrow, actually for other reasons I think he was going to be in Washington, so he's going to come over and see me. That was an example of something where I was kidding, and then people said, 'You know, that's actually a pretty good idea.'" Q: What made you suggest Dana White? Are you serious? Trump: That was an example of something where I was kidding and that people said that's actually pretty good idea pic.twitter.com/8hjBPNNY3K — Acyn (@Acyn) November 8, 2026 Trump caused a stir Saturday when he posted on his Truth Social platform that he was "pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States." The president closed his message with the plea to the UFC executive: "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" White and Trump have maintained a close personal relationship for decades, dating back to the early days of the UFC's rise in the United States, when Trump's Atlantic City hotel and casino hosted two of the promotion's events in 2001. White has since become one of Trump's most prominent supporters in the sports world, speaking at three Republican National Conventions and publicly backing Trump's presidential campaigns. White reacted to Trump's social media post Saturday by posting an image of himself at the podium of the White House press briefing room with the caption, "On to the next chapter." The UFC CEO then told reporters in London that he was "flying to Washington" directly after Zuffa Boxing 12's post-fight press conference in order to meet with Trump. "I've got a lot of jobs already," White said Saturday. "We have a meeting on Monday, so I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that." The White House press secretary position became open just over two weeks ago when Katie Zacharia resigned after only five days on the job . Previously a conservative commentator and adviser for the company that runs Truth Social, Zacharia received immediate scrutiny after an initial press briefing that lasted only five minutes, followed by questions over whether she was actually a lawyer , as claimed. Zacharia took over for Karoline Leavitt, who left the press secretary role in August following the birth of her second child. During Leavitt's maternity leave, other officials in the Trump administration held press briefings, including Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
